The king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, at the valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley).
Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High.
He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth.
Blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Abram gave him a tenth of all.
The king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people, and take the goods for yourself.”
Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth,
that I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap nor anything that is yours, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’
I will accept nothing from you except that which the young men have eaten, and the portion of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them take their portion.”

lifeIntro: This week is about direction more than decisions — which way your tent faces, and whether you are secure enough to be generous.
prayer: Father, show me what my eyes have refused to count. Turn my tent away from Sodom, even if the soil there looks better. Make me secure enough in Your promise to give up a right. Lord Jesus, You lost Your life and were given all things. Make me generous because I am safe in You. Holy Spirit, show me which way my tent is facing today. Amen.

bottomLine: Plenty, not scarcity, caused the conflict, and Abram settled it by giving up a right that was his. Lot lifted his eyes, saw watered land, and never counted the wickedness Genesis names; his tent moved toward Sodom, then into it, and Peter says he was tormented the whole time. Lot chose. Abram was given.
benediction: Brother, if you are in a season of conflict over something you have every right to win — a boundary, an inheritance, a position — look at what Abram did with his rights. He had custom, age, and the promise of God on his side, and he handed the choice to his nephew. He could afford to, because his security did not depend on winning.

Lift up your eyes — that is the phrase the chapter turns on, and it happens twice. Lot lifted his eyes and saw water, and chose, and the choosing cost him nearly everything. Then God told Abram to lift his eyes and look in every direction — not to calculate, but to receive.

Lift up your eyes to the mercy in the warning. Lot was God’s. Peter calls him righteous. He was not God’s enemy. He was a man of God who pitched his tent the wrong way and did not correct it until angels took his hand and pulled him out — “Yahweh being merciful to him.” God pulls His own out of Sodom. He would rather you turned your tent now.

Lift up your eyes and look at your direction this week, not only your decisions. Give away one right you could keep. Let God direct your looking before you weigh anything. He gives what other men have to seize.
closingVerse: Lot chose. Abram was given. That one difference organizes the whole chapter — and much of a life.
carry: Which way is your tent facing right now?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
pulls: Abram names the gap between what God said and what he can see — and brings it to God. That is what faith sounds like under strain.
paras: Genesis 15 opens with God saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward” (Genesis 15:1). That tells you something was frightening him. And Abram, for the first time in the story, pushes back: “Lord Yahweh, what will you give me, since I go childless…?” (Genesis 15:2).

It is a startlingly honest exchange. God has promised offspring like the dust of the earth, and Abram is old, Sarai is barren, and nothing has happened. He does not pretend. He names the gap between what God said and what he can see, and he brings it to God, not to a neighbor. That is not a failure of faith. That is what faith sounds like under strain.

sections.heading: Count the Stars
paras: God does not answer with an argument. He takes Abram outside: “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then, “So your offspring will be” (Genesis 15:5). He answers a question about an empty tent by pointing at a sky. The promise is not made more likely. It is made bigger.

Then comes the verse Paul will build on: “He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Nothing had been done. No child born, no altar built, no law kept, no vow made. A man looked at a sky and believed a promise, and God entered righteousness to his account.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Verb That Changes Everything
paras: The Hebrew verb behind “credited” is ḥāšab, and it can be used of reckoning something to someone’s account. Something Abram did not have was put to his account. Righteousness was not produced by him and then recognized. It was credited to him, and then it was his.

Paul seizes this in Romans 4 and presses the timing: “How then was it counted? When he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision” (Romans 4:10). Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, years later. The sign came after the righteousness, so the righteousness could not have rested on the sign. And it came centuries before the Law. Justification by faith is not a New Testament novelty. It is how God has always dealt with sinners.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Covenant God Walks Alone
paras: Then the chapter does something strange. Abram asks, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?” (Genesis 15:8). God tells him to bring animals, cut them in two, and lay the halves opposite each other. Jeremiah describes the same rite in Israel’s own day: “when they cut the calf in two and passed between its parts” (Jeremiah 34:18). Those who made the covenant walked between the pieces, and the context in Jeremiah makes plain what that meant: the one who broke faith would end like the animals.

At sundown “a deep sleep fell on Abram. Now terror and great darkness fell on him” (Genesis 15:12). Then “a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces” (Genesis 15:17). God passes through. Abram does not. He lies on the ground while God walks the covenant path Himself.

Sit with that. God binds Himself to a covenant that Abram’s children will break again and again, and He walks the path of the curse Himself. Centuries later darkness would cover the land at midday while God’s own Son bore the curse in His body. The torch between the pieces points to a cross.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Faith Is Not a Feeling
paras: Look at what Abram’s faith actually is in this chapter. He questions God twice. He asks for proof. He falls asleep. In the next chapter he will try to secure the promise through Hagar. This is not a man of unwavering calm.

What he does is take God at His word about the future when the present offers nothing to confirm it. Hebrews says it exactly: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Faith is not the absence of questions. It is treating God’s promise as more reliable than your circumstances while the questions are still open.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: Written for You
paras: Paul makes the point personal: “Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone, but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted, who believe in him who raised Jesus, our Lord, from the dead” (Romans 4:23–24).

The same entry is open to you on the same terms. Not because you have produced righteousness, but because it is credited to those who believe. And Paul gives the reason the account balances in the next line: Christ “was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). He was charged with what you owed, and you are credited with what He earned.

stations.question: When God’s promise and your circumstances do not match, do you bring the gap to Him, or carry it in silence and let it sour?
stations.gloss: shield, the protection a man carries
body: Māgēn is a soldier’s shield, the one he carries into the fight. God does not tell Abram, I will give you a shield. He says, “I am your shield.” The protection is not a supply God hands out. It is God Himself, standing between Abram and the threat.
David says the same: “you, Yahweh, are a shield around me, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head” (Psalm 3:3). And the psalmist adds, “Yahweh God is a sun and a shield” (Psalm 84:11).
stations.live: Name the threat you are bracing against, and pray it back to God: You are not sending protection. You are the protection.

stations.verse: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So your offspring will be.
stations.question: Are you measuring God’s promise by what your life shows right now, or letting Him enlarge what you think is possible?
stations.gloss: to count, to number; also to recount, to tell
body: Sāpar means both to count and to tell — the same root behind recounting a story. God tells Abram to count what cannot be counted. A chapter later He promises Hagar offspring that “will not be counted for multitude” (Genesis 16:10).

The psalmist uses the verb for what the sky does: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1). The stars Abram could not count are telling something. What outruns your arithmetic is still preaching.
stations.live: Go outside one night this week, look up, and pray one specific promise of God back to Him under that sky.

stations.verse: He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.
stations.question: Are you trying to produce a righteousness God will recognize, or receiving one He credits to those who believe?
stations.gloss: to reckon, to count as, to credit or impute
body: Ḥāšab is the verb of reckoning — of counting something as something, or putting it to someone’s account. Shimei begs David, “Don’t let my lord impute iniquity to me” (2 Samuel 19:19). David sings the other side of it: “Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity” (Psalm 32:2).

In Genesis 15:6 the entry goes the other way. A righteousness Abram did not have was counted to him because he believed a promise. Paul builds Romans 4 on this verse, and Psalm 32 beside it: sin not counted against you, righteousness counted to you.
stations.live: Stop auditing your record for evidence that God accepts you. Thank Him instead for a righteousness credited, not earned.
pulls: Nothing had been done. A man looked at a sky and believed a promise, and God put righteousness to his account.

stations.question: Are you living as if your standing with God depends on keeping your end, or on the God who walked the covenant path Himself?
stations.gloss: to cut; the verb used for making a covenant
body: In Hebrew you do not simply make a covenant. You cut one. Genesis 15:18 says literally that Yahweh cut a covenant with Abram, and Jeremiah 34:18 shows why: the parties passed between the cut pieces of the calf.

The same verb carries the threat and the mercy. After the flood God promised, “All flesh will not be cut off any more by the waters of the flood” (Genesis 9:11). In Genesis 15 only God passes through, while Abram sleeps. The covenant stands on the One who walked the path, not on the one lying on the ground.
stations.live: When you fear you have forfeited God’s promise by failing, tell yourself the truth: He walked that path Himself. The guarantee is His.

stations.verse: Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform. Therefore it also was “credited to him for righteousness.
stations.question: When you read Genesis 15:6, do you read a fact about Abraham, or an entry Paul says was written with you in view?
stations.gloss: to be fully assured, to be fully convinced
body: Plērophoreō describes something brought to full measure — a mind carried all the way to settled conviction. Paul uses it for a man’s conscience: “Let each man be fully assured in his own mind” (Romans 14:5).

Here it names Abraham: “being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform.” Notice what his assurance rests on. Not on his own strength, which Paul says was “worn out” (Romans 4:19), but on God’s ability. Full assurance is not confidence in yourself. It is confidence in what God said He would do.
stations.live: Write down one promise of God you have been doubting, and under it write Romans 4:21 — then read it each morning this week.

practices.title: BRING THE GAP TO GOD OUT LOUD
practices.body: Abram said it plainly: “what will you give me, since I go childless?” Name the place where God’s promise and your life do not match, and say it to Him directly. Unspoken disappointment does not disappear. It curdles.

practices.title: GO OUTSIDE AND LOOK UP
practices.body: God answered a question about an empty tent by pointing at a sky. Step outside one night this week, look at the stars, and pray one promise back to God under them. Some things cannot be argued into you. They have to be seen.

practices.title: STOP AUDITING YOUR RECORD
practices.body: When you want to know whether God accepts you, your reflex is to review your week. Genesis 15:6 says righteousness was credited to a man who had done nothing but believe. Catch the audit when it starts and replace it: My standing is credited, not earned.

practices.title: REMEMBER WHO WALKED THE PATH
practices.body: Abram lay asleep while God passed between the pieces. When fear rises that you have forfeited God’s promise, answer it with that picture: the guarantee was never mine to keep. He walked it Himself.

practices.title: PUT ONE DEBT WHERE IT BELONGS
practices.body: Name one failure you keep charging back to your own account. Place it where God has already placed it — on Christ, who “was delivered up for our trespasses” — and refuse to move it back.

title: Credited for Righteousness
subtitle: from a childless night to a righteousness God credits
keyVerse: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So your offspring will be.” He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.

passage.text: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”
Abram said, “Lord Yahweh, what will you give me, since I go childless, and he who will inherit my estate is Eliezer of Damascus?”
Abram said, “Behold, you have given no children to me: and, behold, one born in my house is my heir.”
Behold, Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “This man will not be your heir, but he who will come out of your own body will be your heir.”
Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So your offspring will be.”
He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.
He said to Abram, “I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to inherit it.”
He said, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?”
He said to him, “Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.”
He brought him all these, and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other; but he didn’t divide the birds.
The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.
When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. Now terror and great darkness fell on him.
He said to Abram, “Know for sure that your offspring will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them. They will afflict them four hundred years.
I will also judge that nation, whom they will serve. Afterward they will come out with great wealth;
but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried at a good old age.
In the fourth generation they will come here again, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.”
It came to pass that, when the sun went down, and it was dark, behold, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.
In that day Yahweh made a covenant with Abram, saying, “I have given this land to your offspring, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:
the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,
the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,
the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”

Lord Jesus, You were delivered up for my trespasses and raised for my justification. I stop auditing my record and receive what You credit. Holy Spirit, hold my confidence on the promise while my circumstances have not changed. Amen.

bottomLine: Abram brought God an honest complaint about a promise that had not come, and God answered by making the promise bigger. Then a man who had done nothing believed, and God credited it to him for righteousness — before circumcision and centuries before the Law. When Abram asked for assurance, God put him to sleep and walked the covenant path Himself.
benediction: Brother, if you are carrying a promise that has not come — a prayer prayed for years, a hope that has outlived every reasonable timeline — Genesis 15 is your chapter. Abram did not pretend. He said it out loud: “what will you give me, since I go childless?” That honesty was not a failure of faith. It was faith, speaking under strain.

Lift up your eyes — God said it first. He brought Abram outside and told him to look at the stars. He did not make the promise easier to believe. He made it bigger. Sometimes the answer to an impossible situation is not an explanation but a larger sight of the God who made the promise.

Lift up your eyes to the verse the rest of the Bible leans on: “He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.” Nothing had been achieved. A man believed, and God made an entry. Paul says that sentence was written for you as much as for Abraham — same terms, same free crediting of a righteousness you did not produce.

Lift up your eyes to the torch between the pieces. When Abram asked how he would know, God put him to sleep and walked the path Himself. Centuries later, in a darkness at midday, the curse of that covenant fell on the Son. Your standing does not rest on your ability to keep your end. It rests on the God who walked the path alone.
closingVerse: Abram slept while God walked between the pieces. The covenant stands on the One who walked it.
carry: Where are you still trying to produce a righteousness God has already offered to credit?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
pulls: The failure here is not immorality by the world’s measure. It is help God did not ask for.
paras: Ten years have passed since Genesis 12. Ten years of a promise about offspring, and a womb that has stayed closed. Genesis marks the interval on purpose: Sarai gave Hagar to Abram “after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan” (Genesis 16:3). This is not a weak moment after a bad night. It is a decision made after a decade of waiting.

And the plan was not irrational. Sarai says it plainly: “See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her” (Genesis 16:2). A barren wife giving her servant to bear a child in her place was a recognized arrangement in her world. She is not proposing a scandal by the standards around her. She is proposing something sensible. That is what makes the chapter so searching. The failure here is not immorality by the world’s measure. It is help God did not ask for.

sections.heading: The Language of the Garden
paras: Read Genesis 16:2 beside Genesis 3:17 and the echo is hard to miss. To Adam God said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree…” (Genesis 3:17). Of Abram Genesis says, “Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” The narrator is reaching back to Eden.

The point is not to blame the women. In both cases the man is held responsible for what he did with what he heard. The point is that this is the same failure in new clothes. In the garden it was reaching for a good thing on the wrong terms. Here it is reaching for a promised thing on the wrong terms. Sin in Genesis is rarely about wanting bad things. It is about seizing good things ahead of God.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Bitter Harvest of a Sensible Plan
paras: The consequences arrive at once, and Genesis records them with painful realism. Hagar conceives, and “her mistress was despised in her eyes” (Genesis 16:4). Sarai, who devised the plan, now blames Abram: “This wrong is your fault” (Genesis 16:5). Abram washes his hands: “Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes” (Genesis 16:6). “Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face.”

Every relationship in the house is damaged within a few verses: contempt, blame, abdication, cruelty, flight. The plan produced a son, just as intended — and a home where no one could look at anyone. When you take a promise into your own hands, you usually get some version of what you wanted, along with a harvest you did not price in.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The God Who Finds the Runaway
paras: Then the chapter turns, and it turns toward the person with the least standing in it. “Yahweh’s angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness” (Genesis 16:7). Not Abram, the man of the covenant. Not Sarai, the wife of the promise. God goes into the desert after a pregnant Egyptian servant running from a house she did not choose.

And He calls her by name. Sarai and Abram speak of her only as “my servant” and “your maid.” God says, “Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?” (Genesis 16:8). He sends her back with a promise of offspring too many to count, and a son named for what God had done: “You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction” (Genesis 16:11).

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The God Who Sees
paras: Then Hagar does something remarkable. “She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, ‘You are a God who sees’” (Genesis 16:13). In Hebrew it is El Roi. A foreign servant woman in a desert gives God a name, and the name is about being seen. No one else in Scripture is recorded naming God this way.

Think about who was doing the seeing before God came. Sarai saw a problem. Hagar saw an opening, then a rival. Abram saw a way out. No one in that house saw her. The God of heaven went into a wilderness to see a woman no one was looking at, and let her name Him for it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: Waiting Without Manufacturing
paras: Isaac does not arrive for another fourteen years. Abram is eighty-six when Ishmael is born (Genesis 16:16) and a hundred when Isaac is born (Genesis 21:5). Ishmael came from a plan. Isaac would come from a promise. Paul makes that the center of an argument: “the son by the servant was born according to the flesh, but the son by the free woman was born through promise” (Galatians 4:23). The flesh can produce a result. It cannot produce the promise.

So the question this week is not whether you are waiting on something. You are. It is what you are tempted to build while you wait. There is a version of every unanswered prayer that you can arrange for yourself. It will look sensible. It will cost more than you expected. And the people around you will pay part of the bill.

stations.verse: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar. Sarai said to Abram, “See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.” Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
stations.question: In the place you have waited longest, are you still trusting God to keep His word, or quietly arranging a substitute you can produce yourself?
stations.gloss: to hear, to listen, to heed
body: Šāmaʿ means both hearing and heeding. In Hebrew, to listen is to obey. Genesis 16:2 says Abram listened to the voice of Sarai, in the same construction God used of Adam in Genesis 3:17.

Then the verb turns around. The son born of Abram’s listening is named Ishmael — “God hears” — “because Yahweh has heard your affliction” (Genesis 16:11). Abram heeded the wrong voice. God still heard the cry of the one who paid for it. The question is never whether you are listening, but to which voice.
stations.live: Name the voice you have been heeding where you are waiting — your fear, your culture, your own reasoning — and go back to what God actually said.

stations.verse: He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes. Sarai said to Abram, “This wrong is your fault. I gave my servant into your bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, she despised me. May Yahweh judge between me and you.” But Abram said to Sarai, “Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.” Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face.
stations.question: When your own plan goes wrong, do you own it, or look for someone else to carry the blame?
stations.gloss: to be light; to treat as small, to hold in contempt
body: Qālal means to be light. Genesis uses it of the flood going down: “the waters were abated from the earth” (Genesis 8:11). Used of people, it means to treat someone as weightless, of no account. God told Abram He would curse “him who treats you with contempt” (Genesis 12:3), and it is the same verb.

In Genesis 16 Hagar treats Sarai as light, and Sarai answers by treating Hagar harshly. Each makes the other weightless. That is what happens in a house where a promise has been seized instead of received.
stations.live: Name one person you have been treating as weightless, and give him your full, unhurried attention this week.

stations.verse: Yahweh’s angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain on the way to Shur. He said, “Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?” She said, “I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.
stations.question: Do you believe God goes after the overlooked person in the story, or only the one holding the promise?
stations.gloss: to find, to come upon
body: The verb is “found,” and the subject is God. Hagar is not seeking. She is running. Moses uses the same verb for Israel: “He found him in a desert land, in the waste howling wilderness. He surrounded him. He cared for him” (Deuteronomy 32:10).

The initiative in Scripture runs from God toward the one who has fled. Jesus tells of a shepherd who goes after the lost sheep “until he found it” (Luke 15:4). In Genesis 16 the finding comes with a name. God speaks to Hagar as Hagar.
stations.live: Ask God to bring one overlooked person to mind this week, then find him — a call, a visit, a message that uses his name.
pulls: No one in that house saw her. So God went into a wilderness to see her — and let her name Him for it.

stations.verse: She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,” for she said, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?
stations.question: Are you living as if God has overlooked you, or as a man seen by the God Hagar called El Roi?
stations.gloss: God of seeing; the God who sees
body: Rŏʾî is a noun from the verb to see. It can mean sight, or how a thing looks. It describes David’s “good appearance” (1 Samuel 16:12) and, at the other end, Nineveh made “a spectacle” (Nahum 3:6). Joined to ʾēl, God, it names Hagar’s confession: “You are a God who sees.”

Being seen by God can feel like exposure when you are hiding. To someone abandoned in a wilderness, it is comfort. Which one it feels like to you tells you something about where you stand with Him right now.
stations.live: In the place you feel most invisible this week, say it on purpose: You are the God who sees me.

stations.verse: For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the servant, and one by the free woman. However, the son by the servant was born according to the flesh, but the son by the free woman was born through promise.
stations.question: Are you trying to produce by effort what God has said He will give by promise, and calling the result faith?
stations.gloss: promise; an announcement the speaker binds himself to fulfill
body: Epangelia is not a forecast or a possibility. It is a word the speaker binds himself to keep. Paul’s whole contrast in Galatians 4 turns on it: Ishmael came from human ability, Isaac “through promise.” And Paul says the believer stands where Isaac stood: “Now we, brothers, as Isaac was, are children of promise” (Galatians 4:28).
Every such word finds its answer in one Person: “however many are the promises of God, in him is the ‘Yes’” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The flesh can manufacture a result. Only God can deliver a promise.
stations.live: Write down the promise you are waiting on and the substitute you have been tempted to arrange, and hand the second one back to God.

practices.title: NAME YOUR HAGAR
practices.body: Name the substitute you have been arranging where God has seemed slow. It will look sensible, even wise. Write down both: the promise you are waiting on, and the plan you have quietly assembled in case God does not come through.

practices.title: OWN ONE THING YOU ENGINEERED
practices.body: Sarai made the plan and blamed Abram; Abram washed his hands of it. This week, find one mess you helped make and own your part out loud to the person affected — without explaining, softening, or spreading the blame.

practices.title: GIVE WEIGHT TO SOMEONE YOU MADE LIGHT
practices.body: Qālal means to treat as weightless. Pick one person you routinely overlook — a coworker, a relative, someone who serves you — and give him your unhurried, undivided attention this week. Use his name.

practices.title: GO FIND THE RUNAWAY
practices.body: God went into the wilderness after the person with the least standing in the story. Ask God to bring to mind someone who has drifted away or been pushed out, and make real contact this week.

practices.title: SAY EL ROI WHERE YOU FEEL INVISIBLE
practices.body: Hagar named God in the place she was least seen. In your own overlooked place — unnoticed work, unseen faithfulness, private grief — say it: You are the God who sees me.

title: Helping God Keep His Promise
subtitle: from ten years of waiting to a plan of your own making
keyVerse: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar. Sarai said to Abram, “See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.” Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.

passage.text: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.
Sarai said to Abram, “See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.” Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
Sarai, Abram’s wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to Abram her husband to be his wife.
He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.
Sarai said to Abram, “This wrong is your fault. I gave my servant into your bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, she despised me. May Yahweh judge between me and you.”
But Abram said to Sarai, “Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.” Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face.
Yahweh’s angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain on the way to Shur.
He said, “Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?” She said, “I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “I will greatly multiply your offspring, that they will not be counted for multitude.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Behold, you are with child, and will bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction.
He will be like a wild donkey among men. His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him. He will live opposed to all of his brothers.”
She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,” for she said, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?”
Therefore the well was called Beer Lahai Roi. Behold, it is between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore a son for Abram. Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE PLAN AND THE PROMISE
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Hebrew or Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This week is about what you build while you wait, and about the God who goes into wildernesses after people no one is looking for.
prayer: Father, keep me from building what only You can give. I confess the substitutes I have arranged while I waited. Lord Jesus, You are the “Yes” to every promise of God. I wait on You, not around You. Holy Spirit, open my eyes to the person no one is seeing, and let me see him the way You see me. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, keep me from building what only You can give.
I confess the substitutes I have arranged while I waited.
Lord Jesus, You are the “Yes” to every promise of God.
I wait on You, not around You.
Holy Spirit, open my eyes to the person no one is seeing,
and let me see him the way You see me.
Amen.
bottomLine: After ten years of waiting, Sarai proposed a respectable solution and Abram listened — in words that echo Adam in the garden. The plan worked, and the household broke. Then God went into the wilderness after the least regarded person in the story, called her by name, and she named Him El Roi, the God who sees.
benediction: Brother, if you have been waiting a long time — long enough that you have started sketching a plan of your own, long enough that the sensible substitute has begun to look like wisdom instead of unbelief — Genesis 16 was written with you in view. Ten years is a long time to hold a promise with nothing to show for it.

Lift up your eyes and see how respectable the failure was. Sarai proposed nothing her world would have called wrong. It was a reasonable answer to an unreasonable delay, and it produced a son, just as designed — along with contempt, blame, cruelty, and a woman running into a desert. The flesh can give you a result. It cannot give you the promise, and it always sends someone else the bill.

Lift up your eyes to the God who goes into the wilderness. When the house broke and the least important person in it fled, God went after her — not after Abram, not after Sarai, but after a pregnant Egyptian servant. He called her by her name, which no one in that house had done.

Lift up your eyes to the name she gave Him. If your faithfulness is unnoticed and your grief is private, and you have begun to suspect God has moved on to more important matters, hear what a runaway servant said at a desert spring: “You are a God who sees.” He sees you in the waiting. He will keep His word.
closingVerse: The flesh can produce a result. It cannot produce the promise.
carry: What are you tempted to build while you wait on God?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
pulls: God waited until the promise was humanly impossible before He moved. The delay was not indifference. It was clarity.
paras: Thirteen years separate the end of Genesis 16 from the start of Genesis 17. Abram is eighty-six when Ishmael is born (Genesis 16:16) and ninety-nine when God speaks again. Ishmael has grown into a young man, and the text records no word from God in between. Abram arranged a solution, and heaven was quiet. Then, when every natural possibility has closed, God speaks.

The timing is part of the message. God waited until the promise was humanly impossible before He moved. Paul says so: Abraham “didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb” (Romans 4:19). The delay was not indifference. It made sure that when the child came, no one could mistake where he came from.

sections.heading: God Almighty and a New Name
paras: God introduces Himself with a title Scripture uses here for the first time: “I am God Almighty” — in Hebrew, El Shaddai. To a man whose body is spent, He announces Himself by His sufficiency. Then come two commands: “Walk before me and be blameless” (Genesis 17:1). The first is about direction: live your whole life in His presence, under His eye. The second is about wholeness: not sinlessness, but an undivided life.

Then God changes his name: “Your name will no more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations” (Genesis 17:5). Consider the timing. He is ninety-nine, with no son by Sarai, and God renames him father of a multitude. Every time he introduced himself for the rest of his life, he said out loud a promise he could not yet see.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Obedience as Response, Not Payment
paras: The order in this chapter matters as much as it did in Genesis 15. Righteousness was credited to Abram in chapter 15, before any sign and before any command to walk blamelessly. In chapter 17 God gives commands and a sign. The obedience comes after the crediting, so it is a response and not a payment.

Paul presses the order because everything rests on it. If circumcision had come first, righteousness would be a wage. Because it came second, righteousness is a gift and circumcision is a seal on it. Get the order backward and you have a different religion. James is not arguing otherwise when he says faith without works is dead. He is describing the same fruit from the other side.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A Sign in the Flesh
paras: The sign God chooses is startling: “Every male among you shall be circumcised… It will be a token of the covenant between me and you” (Genesis 17:10–11). Cut into the body, permanent, private, and placed at the very organ of generation. God marks the covenant at the place the promised offspring would come from. Every Israelite man carried in his body a reminder that the line belonged to God.

The prophets made clear that the outward mark was never the point. Moses tells Israel, “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked” (Deuteronomy 10:16). Paul finishes the thought: “circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit not in the letter” (Romans 2:29). The sign always pointed past itself to a cleansing only God could do.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Where the Cutting Landed
paras: Colossians ties the thread to Christ: “In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith” (Colossians 2:11–12). The mark that once set apart God’s people is fulfilled in a death and a resurrection.

Circumcision was a cutting off. At the cross Christ was cut off entirely, bearing in Himself the penalty for every covenant His people broke. The sign in Abraham’s flesh looked ahead to a Person who would be cut off for the flesh of all His people.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: Walking Before a God Who Sees Everything
paras: So what does it mean to walk before God? Not to perform for Him, and not to earn His approval — that was settled in chapter 15. It means living without a backstage. Most men keep two lives: the one others see and the one they live in private. “Walk before me” collapses the two. The God who saw Hagar in the wilderness sees you in your house.

And notice that God gives the command after He gives the name. He does not say, walk blamelessly and then I will make you a father of nations. He says who He is, renames Abram, and sets the covenant — and the walking flows from the identity instead of earning it. You do not walk to earn a name. You walk because you have one.

stations.verse: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless. I will make my covenant between me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly.
stations.question: Are you living one life in public and another in private, or walking before a God who sees both as one?
stations.gloss: blameless, whole, complete; without defect
body: Tāmîm does not mean sinless. It means whole, undivided. It is used of sacrificial animals without defect, and of Noah, “blameless among the people of his time” (Genesis 6:9), who was plainly not perfect. The psalmist asks who may dwell with God, and answers: “He who walks blamelessly and does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart” (Psalm 15:2).
The opposite of tāmîm is not failure. It is a divided life — one split into compartments. God is not asking Abraham for perfection. He is asking for one life instead of two.
stations.live: Name one area where your public self and private self do not match, and begin to close the gap this week by telling one man the truth.

stations.verse: God said to Abraham, “As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but her name will be Sarah. I will bless her, and moreover I will give you a son by her. Yes, I will bless her, and she will be a mother of nations. Kings of peoples will come from her.
stations.question: Are you defining yourself by what is visible in your life right now, or by the name God has already given you?
stations.gloss: Sarah; the name sounds the word for princess
body: God renames the wife as well as the husband. Sarai becomes Sarah, and the new name sounds the Hebrew word for a woman of royal rank, the word used of Solomon’s “princesses” (1 Kings 11:3). Then God adds a promise no one had spoken before: “she will be a mother of nations. Kings of peoples will come from her” (Genesis 17:16).

In a chapter often read only for the patriarch, God stops to give a barren ninety-year-old woman a new name and a royal future. Peter later holds her up to believing women as a model of hope (1 Peter 3:6).
stations.live: Ask God what He calls you, and answer the accusing voice this week with that name, not with your record.

stations.verse: God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you.
stations.question: Are you treating the outward marks of faith as the substance, or as signs pointing to what only God can do in you?
stations.gloss: sign, token; a mark that points beyond itself
body: An ʾôt is never the thing itself. It points. The rainbow was the sign of the covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:13). The Sabbath was a sign at Sinai: “it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations” (Exodus 31:13). Circumcision is the sign here.
Signs go wrong the moment they are mistaken for the substance. That is what happened in Israel, and it is what Paul spends much of Romans arguing against.
stations.live: Name one religious habit you have been leaning on, and trace it back to the reality it was meant to point you to.
pulls: He was ninety-nine, with no son by Sarah, and God renamed him father of a multitude. Every introduction after that was an act of faith.

stations.verse: He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while he was in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all those who believe, though they might be in uncircumcision, that righteousness might also be accounted to them. He is the father of circumcision to those who not only are of the circumcision, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham, which he had in uncircumcision.
stations.question: Do you believe God accepts you because of the sign you carry, or that the sign only sealed what faith had already received?
stations.gloss: seal; a mark of ownership and authenticity
body: A sphragis was pressed into wax to authenticate a document and declare its owner. Paul tells the Corinthians, “you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 9:2). And God’s foundation stands, “having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are his’” (2 Timothy 2:19).

Paul says circumcision was “a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while he was in uncircumcision.” The seal did not create the reality. It certified it. And the mark of ownership has moved from the flesh to a Person: believers were “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13).
stations.live: When you doubt your standing this week, stop looking for proof in your performance and ask instead: whose seal am I carrying?

stations.verse: In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
stations.question: Are you still trying to cut away your own flesh by discipline, or trusting a cutting Christ has already done in you?
stations.gloss: not made with hands; done by God alone
body: Acheiropoiētos marks what only God can make. At Jesus’ trial the witnesses quote Him speaking of a temple “made without hands” (Mark 14:58). Paul uses it of the body that awaits believers, “a house not made with hands, eternal, in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1). Here it is a circumcision done by Christ, not by a knife.
The decisive cutting away of the flesh is not something you achieve by discipline. It was done to you, in Him, when you were buried and raised with Him.
stations.live: Stop trying to cut away a stubborn sin by willpower alone. Confess it as a man already buried and raised with Christ, and ask Him to make that true in you.

practices.title: CLOSE ONE GAP
practices.body: Tāmîm means undivided, not sinless. Name one place where the man others see does not match the man at home or online, and begin to close it this week by telling one trustworthy man the truth.

practices.title: ANSWER THE ACCUSATION WITH YOUR NAME
practices.body: God renamed a childless ninety-nine-year-old father of a multitude. When the accusing voice tells you what you are, answer with what God calls you — forgiven, son, His. Say it out loud. The name was given before the evidence arrived.

practices.title: TRACE ONE PRACTICE TO ITS REALITY
practices.body: Signs go wrong when they become the substance. Pick one habit you lean on — attendance, giving, a reading plan — and ask what it points to. Then give your attention to the reality this week, not only the marker.

practices.title: WAIT WHERE IT HAS BECOME IMPOSSIBLE
practices.body: God moved when Abraham’s body was “worn out.” If you are in a situation past natural possibility, resist the urge to close the file. That is where God has acted before.

practices.title: STOP CUTTING WHAT CHRIST HAS CUT
practices.body: Name the sin you have been fighting by discipline alone. Confess it this week as flesh already cut away in Christ, and ask the Spirit to make what is true of you real in you.

title: Walk Before Me
subtitle: from Abram to Abraham, and a covenant marked in the flesh
keyVerse: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless. I will make my covenant between me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly.

passage.text: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless.
I will make my covenant between me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly.”
Abram fell on his face. God talked with him, saying,
“As for me, behold, my covenant is with you. You will be the father of a multitude of nations.
Your name will no more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make nations of you. Kings will come out of you.
I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your offspring after you.
I will give to you, and to your offspring after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations.
This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised.
You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you.
He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring.
He who is born in your house, and he who is bought with your money, must be circumcised. My covenant will be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant.
The uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people. He has broken my covenant.”
God said to Abraham, “As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but her name will be Sarah.
I will bless her, and moreover I will give you a son by her. Yes, I will bless her, and she will be a mother of nations. Kings of peoples will come from her.”
Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, “Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”
Abraham said to God, “Oh that Ishmael might live before you!”
God said, “No, but Sarah, your wife, will bear you a son. You shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.

As for Ishmael, I have heard you. Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly. He will become the father of twelve princes, and I will make him a great nation.
But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this set time next year.”
When he finished talking with him, God went up from Abraham.

Abraham took Ishmael his son, all who were born in his house, and all who were bought with his money: every male among the men of Abraham’s house, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskin in the same day, as God had said to him.
Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.
Ishmael, his son, was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.
In the same day both Abraham and Ishmael, his son, were circumcised.
All the men of his house, those born in the house, and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON WALKING BEFORE GOD
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Hebrew or Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This week is about one undivided life, a new name, and a sign that always pointed past itself.
prayer: Father, You are God Almighty. I walk before You today — no backstage, no second life. You named me before the evidence arrived. Lord Jesus, You were cut off so that I could be made whole. Do in me what my discipline never could. Holy Spirit, You are the seal of God’s ownership. Remind me whose mark I carry when I doubt. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, You are God Almighty.
I walk before You today — no backstage, no second life.
You named me before the evidence arrived.
Lord Jesus, You were cut off so that I could be made whole.
Do in me what my discipline never could.
Holy Spirit, You are the seal of God’s ownership.
Remind me whose mark I carry when I doubt.
Amen.
bottomLine: After thirteen years of silence, God spoke when Abraham was ninety-nine and introduced Himself as God Almighty. He called for an undivided life, renamed a childless man father of a multitude, renamed his barren wife, and gave a sign in the flesh. But the order is everything: righteousness was credited in chapter 15, and the sign came in chapter 17 — a seal, not a wage.
benediction: Brother, thirteen years of silence is a long time. Abram arranged a solution in Genesis 16, and heaven was quiet long enough for a boy to grow into a young man. If you are in a stretch where God has seemed silent since the last time you took matters into your own hands, you are on familiar ground.

Lift up your eyes to when God finally spoke. Not while Abraham was still capable. He waited until the man was ninety-nine and his wife was ninety and the thing was finished by every human measure. That is not God being slow. That is God making sure that when Isaac arrived, no one could mistake whose son he was.

Lift up your eyes to what God did before He asked anything. He named Himself God Almighty. He gave a new name to a man with no son by Sarah and a royal name to a woman with a closed womb. Only then did He say, “Walk before me.” The name came first, and the walking flowed from it.

Lift up your eyes to the cutting not made with hands. When you fight the flesh this week, remember that the decisive cut was done in Christ, and you were buried and raised with Him. Live one life, not two. The God who renamed Abraham before the evidence arrived has named you too.
closingVerse: The name came first, and the walking flowed from it. You do not walk to earn a name. You walk because you have one.
carry: Where are you still keeping a second life out of God’s sight?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
pulls: If the patriarchs are the point, Genesis is a catalog of failures. They are not the hero of the book. They are the reason it needed one.
paras: Twelve weeks ago you started with a void and a voice. You finish by looking back down the road, because Genesis 1–17 is not a collection of episodes. It is one thread, and the thread has a name.

The dust’s last lie is that all of this is about you — that Scripture is a manual for self-improvement, that the patriarchs are role models, that the point of Genesis is to be more like Abraham. But Abraham passed off his wife as his sister to save his own skin, arranged a son through a servant, and laughed at God’s promise. Noah ended up drunk in his tent. Adam blamed his wife. Cain would not answer God at all. If these men are the point, the book is a catalog of failures.

sections.heading: Tracing the Thread
paras: Follow it from the beginning. In Eden God promises an offspring who will crush the serpent’s head and be wounded doing it: “He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). Then, before the man and woman leave the garden, “Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21). A life is taken so the guilty can be covered, in the third chapter of the Bible.

Then the thread narrows. From all mankind to Noah, carried through judgment in a ship God shut Himself. From the scattered nations at Babel to one man from Ur. From Abram it will narrow to Isaac, the son of promise, not of the flesh. Genesis keeps closing off alternatives until one line remains, and Paul names it: “Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He doesn’t say, ‘To descendants’, as of many, but as of one, ‘To your offspring’, which is Christ” (Galatians 3:16).

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Every Pattern Points the Same Way
paras: Look at what has piled up over eleven weeks. A word spoken into a void, and a Word made flesh who shines in dark hearts. Breath given to lifeless dust, and a risen Christ breathing on His disciples with the verb the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7. A covering bought with a life, and a Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

Blood that cries from the ground for justice, and blood of sprinkling that speaks better than Abel’s. A ship that goes through judgment, not around it, and a baptism Peter says answers to it. A name men grasped for and lost, a name given freely to Abram, and at last the name above every name, given to the One who went down. A covenant God walked alone in the dark, and a darkness at midday when the curse fell on His Son.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Wound Inside the Promise
paras: Go back to Genesis 3:15 and notice that the victory is announced with an injury built into it. The serpent is crushed, but the offspring is wounded in the crushing. From the first promise God told you that rescue would cost the Rescuer.

That is the shape of everything after it: an animal dies so Adam can be clothed; a ram is caught in a thicket so Isaac can go free (Genesis 22:13); a covenant is guaranteed by a God who walks between the pieces alone. From Genesis 3 on, the Bible announces that God will save at His own expense. When the moment came, the wounds were in His hands and feet.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: From Dust to Resurrection
paras: The title of this study has four beats, and the last one is not the end of the sentence. Dust, breath, fall, promise — and the promise leads somewhere. Paul finishes it: “The first man is of the earth, made of dust. The second man is the Lord from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:47). And in the same chapter, “the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we will be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

The dust you came from is not your destiny. “For you are dust, and you shall return to dust” (Genesis 3:19) is true, but it is not the whole truth, because the God who breathed into dust once has bound Himself to do it finally. Ezekiel saw a valley of dry bones stand up. Christ walked out of a tomb. The resurrection is Genesis 2:7 done on a scale that will include your body.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: How to Read the Rest of Your Bible
paras: So take this past week twelve. When you open the Old Testament, the first question is not only what you must do, but where the promised offspring is. Jesus set that pattern on the Emmaus road: “Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). He began with Moses. He began with Genesis.

You are dust — finite, mortal, formed from the ground, and God remembers it with compassion. You are breathed into — carrying a life you did not make. You are fallen — and the ground still bears the marks. And you are promised — because before the man and woman left Eden, God announced an offspring who would crush the serpent’s head. That is the whole arc, and it has a name.

stations.verse: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.
stations.question: Have you been reading Scripture mainly to find out what you must do, or to find the One God promised before Eden was lost?
stations.gloss: to bruise, to crush, to strike
body: Genesis 3:15 uses the same verb for both blows. The offspring bruises the serpent’s head; the serpent bruises his heel. The same action, but where it lands decides the outcome: a crushed head is the end, a wounded heel is not.

Job uses the verb of God’s dealings with him: “he breaks me with a storm” (Job 9:17). Paul echoes Genesis 3:15 with a different Greek verb when he promises, “the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). The victory of the offspring is shared with everyone joined to Him.
stations.live: When you are wounded in obedience this week, name it honestly: this is a heel, not a head. The outcome is settled.

stations.verse: Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
stations.question: Are you still stitching a covering of your own, or wearing the one God provided at the cost of a life?
stations.gloss: tunic, a long garment
body: Kətōnet is the word behind “garments” in Genesis 3:21. It is the tunic Jacob gave Joseph, “a tunic of many colors” (Genesis 37:3). It is also the high priest’s garment on the Day of Atonement: “He shall put on the holy linen tunic” (Leviticus 16:4).

The first garment in the Bible is God’s gift to guilty people, and the word later clothes the priest who goes in to make atonement. From Eden to the tabernacle, the covering that saves is one God specifies and God provides.
stations.live: Thank God this week, specifically, that your covering cost Him a life so that it would not cost you yours.

stations.verse: Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He doesn’t say, “To descendants”, as of many, but as of one, “To your offspring”, which is Christ.
stations.question: Do you see the Old Testament as a separate story that ended, or as a promise whose single thread runs to Christ?
stations.gloss: seed, offspring
body: Sperma is the Greek word the Greek Old Testament uses for zeraʿ in Genesis 3:15. Paul builds an argument on its number, and it is not a trick. Genesis itself works the difference between offspring as many and offspring as one.

The line narrows steadily: from mankind to Noah, to Abraham, to Isaac, and later to David, until one offspring remains. Paul says the gospel concerns God’s Son, “who was born of the offspring of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). Paul is reading Genesis the way Genesis asks to be read.
stations.live: Read one Genesis story this week tracing the promised line, and notice where the story narrows instead of widens.
pulls: From the first promise, God announced that rescue would cost the Rescuer. The head would be crushed, and the heel wounded doing it.

stations.verse: The first man is of the earth, made of dust. The second man is the Lord from heaven. As is the one made of dust, such are those who are also made of dust; and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let’s also bear the image of the heavenly.
stations.question: Are you living as though dust is your destiny, or as a man who will be raised?
stations.gloss: made of dust, earthy
body: Choïkos is built on chous, loose earth — the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7 for the dust God formed the man from. Paul uses choïkos for Adam and for everyone who comes from him: “The first man is of the earth, made of dust.”

But he does not leave you there. The second Man is “the Lord from heaven,” and Paul calls you to “bear the image of the heavenly.” The dust is your origin and your present. Scripture will not let it be your end.
stations.live: When your body fails you this week — fatigue, sickness, age — say it on purpose: this is the dust image. It is not the last one.

stations.verse: Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
stations.question: When you open the Old Testament, are you looking mainly for a rule to follow, or for the Christ who said it was about Him?
stations.gloss: to explain, to interpret, to translate
body: Diermēneuō means to carry meaning fully across — to explain thoroughly, or to translate. Luke uses it of a name, “Tabitha, which when translated, means Dorcas” (Acts 9:36). Paul uses it of interpreting tongues (1 Corinthians 12:30).

On the Emmaus road Jesus does this with the whole Old Testament, beginning with Moses — which means He began with Genesis. He treated the book you have spent twelve weeks in as being about Himself from its first pages.
stations.live: Pick the next Old Testament book you will read, and at every chapter ask: how does this prepare me to recognize Christ?

practices.title: READ GENESIS 3:15 AS THE HINGE
practices.body: Go back to the promise spoken before the man and woman left Eden, and read the whole study in its light. Write two or three sentences on where you now see that promise running through the chapters you have read.

practices.title: CHANGE THE FIRST QUESTION
practices.body: This week, open an Old Testament passage and ask where the promised offspring is before you ask what you must do. The second question is right. It is the second one. Jesus showed the order on the Emmaus road.

practices.title: NAME THE BEAT YOU ARE IN
practices.body: Dust, breath, fall, promise. Which one honestly describes your season — frailty, gift, failure, or waiting? Say it to God plainly, and let the next beat be your prayer.

practices.title: TELL THE THREAD TO ONE MAN
practices.body: The promise was always “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” Find one man this week and tell him, in ordinary words, one thing you have seen in Genesis about who Christ is.

practices.title: KEEP AN ALTAR AND A TENT
practices.body: Abram marked his life with both — a fixed place of worship and a loose grip on everything else. Decide now what your altar will be after this study ends, and name one thing you will keep holding like a tent.

title: The Offspring Who Was Promised
subtitle: from the dust of Eden to the Son who crushes the serpent
keyVerse: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.

passage.text: Yahweh God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed above all livestock, and above every animal of the field. You shall go on your belly and you shall eat dust all the days of your life.
I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. You will bear children in pain. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life.
It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.
You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the ground, for you were taken out of it. For you are dust, and you shall return to dust.”
The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living.
Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE PROMISED OFFSPRING
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Hebrew or Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just read.
lifeIntro: This last week is about carrying the thread with you — reading the rest of your Bible, and the rest of your life, in light of the promised offspring.
prayer: Father, You spoke an offspring over the wreckage before the man and woman left the garden. I live under that promise today. Lord Jesus, every thread in Genesis runs to You. You took the wound and crushed the head. Let me see You whenever I read. Holy Spirit, do in me what You did in the dust at the beginning, and raise this dust on the last day. Amen.

bottomLine: Genesis 1–17 is one thread, not a string of episodes. The promised offspring is announced in Eden, a covering is made from a life, and the line narrows until Paul names the one offspring: Christ. The patriarchs are not the hero of the book; they are the reason it needed one.
benediction: Brother, you started twelve weeks ago with a void and a voice, and you end here, looking back down the road. You have walked through creation and collapse, through a flood and a tower, through a call and a covenant and a wilderness where God found a runaway servant. If you read carefully, you noticed that the men in these stories are more often to be pitied than copied.

Lift up your eyes, because that was always the design. Abraham lied, schemed, and laughed. Noah ended his story drunk. Adam blamed his wife, and Cain would not answer. They are not the hero. They are the reason the story needed one.

Lift up your eyes to the hero announced in chapter three, before the man and woman left Eden: “He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.” An offspring is coming, and crushing the serpent will cost Him a wound. Watch the line narrow — from mankind to one family in a ship, from the scattered nations to one man from Ur, from Ishmael to Isaac, from the flesh to the promise — until Paul says the name out loud: the offspring is Christ.

Lift up your eyes from the dust to the One who took on flesh for it, was wounded for it, and was raised out of it. You are dust, and God remembers it with compassion. You are breathed into. You are fallen, and no fig leaf has ever covered it. And you are promised — and the Son who crushed the serpent’s head will one day breathe on your dust the way God breathed in Eden, and raise you.
closingVerse: You are dust, and breathed into, and fallen, and promised. The last word over your life is the one God spoke first.
carry: What one thing from these twelve weeks will you carry into your next reading of Scripture?
